# Mermaid Charts: Accessibility, Renderer Security, and Portability

## Scope

This document explains what mermaid emits, which parts of a chart reach assistive technology, why clickable navigation fails in several common renderers, and what to do instead. It is the reference behind the rules in *Style Guide: Markdown Mermaid Navigation Flowcharts and Linked Sections*, which governs the pattern itself.

The short version: a mermaid chart is a picture, not a structure. Treat it as decoration, put the real content and navigation in markup beside it, and post-process the SVG so it describes itself as one image.

## What mermaid emits

A mermaid chart passes through several distinct mechanisms, and they fail independently. Knowing which is which explains nearly every surprise.

**The graphic.** An `<svg>` element containing shapes, paths, and text.

**Node labels.** By default these are HTML wrapped in a `<foreignObject>` element rather than SVG text. This is configurable.

**The accessible title and description.** `accTitle` and `accDescr` become a real `<title>` and `<desc>` element inside the `<svg>`, wired up with `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby`. Mermaid also sets `aria-roledescription` to the diagram type automatically <a id="ref-mermaid-a11y"></a>[(Mermaid, n.d.-a)](#mermaid-a11y).

**Click targets.** A `click` line either binds a JavaScript navigation function or, with the `href` keyword, produces an anchor-like link.

**Node tooltips.** Not what they appear to be. See below.

## Tooltips do not work the way the syntax suggests

Reading the mermaid source settles a question that documentation does not <a id="ref-mermaid-src"></a>[(Mermaid, 2026)](#mermaid-src).

The tooltip on a `click` line is written to the node group as a `title` **attribute**: `el.attr("title", node.tooltip)`. In SVG, a `title` attribute is inert. It is an HTML attribute with no meaning on SVG elements, so no browser renders a native tooltip from it and no assistive technology reads it as an accessible name.

Mermaid compensates in JavaScript. A `setupToolTips` routine binds mouseover and mouseout handlers to every `g.node`, reads that inert attribute, and displays the text in a `div.mermaidTooltip` appended to `document.body`, absolutely positioned, with `pointer-events: none`. Mouse-only, JavaScript-only, and living outside the SVG entirely.

`accTitle` behaves differently, because it produces a real `<title>` element as the first child of the `<svg>`. Browsers render an SVG `<title>` element as a native tooltip for its parent, and that parent is the whole graphic.

This produces a useful diagnostic. **If every node in a chart shows the same tooltip, and that text is the `accTitle`, then the per-node tooltip binding is not running at all.** Either the renderer stripped the click directives, or the SVG is static with no mermaid runtime attached. In a build-time rendering pipeline that state is permanent by design.

The practical conclusion: a tooltip on a `click` line is not a label for assistive technology and should never be relied on as one.

## What reaches assistive technology

Very little, by default.

Mermaid sets `aria-roledescription` and, when the author supplies them, the accessible title and description. That is the whole of it. The diagram content itself is essentially inaccessible to screen readers, and mermaid's own issue tracker states that it typically presents as near-nonsense, because a reader encounters scattered label text with no information about which node connects to which <a id="ref-mermaid-sr"></a>[(Mermaid, 2024)](#mermaid-sr).

This is worse than it sounds. An SVG contains real text, which seems like an advantage over a raster image, but unstructured exposed text is worse than none: the reader receives a jumble of words with no signal that it is a jumble.

Two further problems. Mermaid emits its own styling, so a diagram does not follow a user's contrast or colour preferences. And no SVG diagram reflows when text is enlarged, since the layout is fixed inside the viewBox.

## Why links fail in GitHub and Obsidian

The default `click NODE "#target" "Tooltip"` form navigates through a JavaScript binding. That is what breaks.

**GitHub** sends a strict Content Security Policy, which is an HTTP header telling the browser what it may load and execute. GitHub's policy blocks mermaid's click navigation, so clicking a node produces a blocked-content message rather than a jump. The reported workaround is to place an anchor inside the node label, because the `click` command cannot make a whole node clickable under that policy <a id="ref-gh-csp"></a>[(GitHub Community, 2023)](#gh-csp).

**Obsidian** strips the native binding for the same class of reason. At least one plugin reimplements click-to-navigate with its own handling specifically because Obsidian's security settings can remove mermaid's binding, and because that binding cannot resolve wiki links in any case <a id="ref-obsidian"></a>[(obsidian-mermaid-flow, 2025)](#obsidian).

**A static build** removes the runtime entirely, so a JavaScript binding is dead markup. An `href` anchor is ordinary navigation and survives all three cases, along with any CSP a published site later adopts.

## Why HTML labels break every non-browser target

The anchor-in-label workaround requires HTML labels, and HTML labels require `<foreignObject>`, which only browsers understand.

The mermaid-cli bug report on missing labels was closed with the explanation that supporting `foreignObject` would mean embedding a whole HTML renderer inside librsvg, and the recommendation to emit SVG text elements instead <a id="ref-mmdc"></a>[(mermaid-cli, n.d.)](#mmdc). One documentation plugin disables HTML labels by default because PDF generation tools cannot render them and the text simply disappears, leaving empty boxes <a id="ref-mkdocs"></a>[(mkdocs-mermaid-to-svg, n.d.)](#mkdocs).

So the label anchor buys the best browser accessibility and costs every other output format. For a pipeline that also emits PDF or EPUB from the same source, that trade goes the wrong way.

Disable HTML labels at the top level of the configuration, not only under the diagram key, and labels render as native SVG `<text>`. This has a second benefit: an unclosed `<br>` inside an HTML label makes the SVG invalid XML, so it fails to load in any strict parser.

## The conflict that decides the approach

The standard fix for the content jumble is to stop pretending the graphic is readable structure and treat it as one described image: `role="img"` on the root, `aria-labelledby` pointing at the title and description, and the internal text hidden from assistive technology. The reader then gets one coherent description instead of fragments.

That treatment hides any links inside the graphic along with everything else. A diagram cannot be both a coherently described image and a set of individually announced clickable nodes.

Resolve it by moving the navigation out of the picture. The chart becomes decoration, and a parallel list of links beside it does the work. The list is keyboard operable, announced as a link list, works with no JavaScript, survives any CSP, survives static rendering, and works in a text browser or a PDF. A nested list also carries the relationships that mermaid cannot express, since indentation is structure a screen reader announces.

## Recommended practice

**Render at build time.** No runtime dependency, no layout shift, no JavaScript required to read a diagram, and the SVG sits in the HTML where a text browser or a PDF emitter can find it.

**Disable HTML labels**, at the top level of the configuration.

**Use no `<br/>` and no escaped `\n` in labels.** Put continuation text on the next source line. This keeps labels readable in the source, keeps the SVG valid XML, and keeps it portable to non-browser renderers.

**Write a short `accTitle`.** It is both the accessible name and the native hover text for the entire graphic, so a long one becomes noise on every hover.

**Write an `accDescr` that describes relationships**, not just the list of node names. It is the only thing a screen reader receives from the graphic, so it should say what the picture shows that a list does not: where the flow branches, what depends on what. Where a parallel list follows the chart, say so in one clause, because a reader who receives only the description has no other way to know the stages are individually reachable.

**Use the `href` click form.** `click NODE href "#target" "Tooltip"` produces markup rather than a JavaScript binding.

**Put a parallel list of the same links beside the chart**, in the same order, nested to match the structure. This is the actual navigation.

**Describe complex diagrams in prose**, or as a table where the content is really tabular.

**State each stage's position in its own section.** Where boxes lead to sections, the relationships live only in the picture and in the indentation of the list, and both of those are the same claim made twice. Fold each section's position into its opening sentence, so the structure survives in prose for a reader who has neither. Avoid a separate previous-and-next line: it becomes boilerplate readers learn to skip, and it duplicates what the list already carries structurally.

**Expose the mermaid source**, in a `details` element or as a sidecar file. Structured text that states relationships explicitly is arguably the most accessible representation on offer, and it keeps the diagram editable.

## Post-processing the SVG

One transform, written once, applied to every diagram on every site. This is the step that is impossible when a CMS owns the rendering path.

The transform should set `role="img"` on the root SVG, point `aria-labelledby` at the `<title>` and `<desc>` already generated from `accTitle` and `accDescr`, hide the internal text from assistive technology, and strip or remap the inline styling so user contrast preferences apply.

It should also convert each inert `title` attribute into a real `<title>` element inside its node group. Innermost wins, so hovering a node then shows that node's own text rather than the diagram title, and it works with no JavaScript, no CDN and no runtime. This recovers the behaviour the click tooltips were supposed to provide, in static markup.

## Multilingual note

A diagram belongs to an expression, not to a work. Node labels, `accTitle` and `accDescr` are all translatable prose. A single rendered diagram shared across language versions would leave its accessible text in one language while the page around it declares another.

## The cost of three representations

Following the rules above puts the same relationships in three places: the diagram, the list, and the section prose. Three places is three chances to drift.

That cost is worth paying, because no single representation reaches everyone. It does mean the sync check is no longer optional, and it is a poor fit for human memory. Every box should have a list entry, every list entry a section, and every click target should resolve. Those are mechanical checks, better run by the toolchain than remembered by an author.

## Verification

Check each of these before publishing a chart.

| Check | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| JavaScript disabled | Diagram still renders, links still work |
| Screen reader | One coherent description, not scattered labels |
| Keyboard only | Every destination reachable through the parallel list |
| Hover a node | That node's own text, not the diagram title |
| Non-browser renderer | Labels present, not empty boxes |
| Text enlarged | Content still reachable through the list and prose |
| Source | Retrievable and editable |
| Section prose | Each stage's position in the flow stated, not only drawn |
| Sync | Every box has a list entry, every list entry a section, every click target resolves |
